transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-21
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood), Maya Chen (AtlasHealth Head of ML), Carlos Rivera (Platform Eng), Anita Gupta (Security)

Auto-summary: Technical deep dive on multi-region routing, failover playbooks, and policy-driven routing for latency/cost tradeoffs. Covered regional capacity planning, DR test cadence, VPC/on-prem constraints, KV cache implications across regions, and quantization/throughput impacts. Agreed next steps: share design doc, run staged DR test, and share cost model.

[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick intros?
[00:07] Maya Chen: Hi, Maya here, Head of ML at AtlasHealth, we run patient-facing summarization and some clinical search.
[00:12] Carlos Rivera: Carlos, platform team, I manage infra and networking.
[00:15] Anita Gupta: Anita, security and compliance.
[00:17] Priya Shah: Priya from Redwood, I'll lead the technical portion.
[00:20] Liam O'Connor: Liam here, solutions engineering.
[00:22] Jordan Lee: Cool. High-level goal for this session is to walk through multi-region routing and failover -- policies, capacity, DR playbooks, and specific impacts on latency and KV cache.

[03:10] Priya Shah: So starting with routing model. We typically recommend a policy-based approach: prefer-region for latency-sensitive traffic, cost-based fallback to cheaper region variants, and a capacity-aware fallback that can route to Redwood Dedicated pools or Redwood Private if hosted capacity's saturated. Note: some words in the diagram might show Redwood Dedicate in the exported slide, sorry for the typo.

[06:02] Maya Chen: Couple of constraints from our side: PHI data must not leave region-us-east-1 for some datasets, and anything that touches PHI needs KMS-managed keys under our control. How do we do regional routing without violating that?
[06:32] Priya Shah: Good question. You can set route policies per model or per route so PHI routes pin to a private deployment in us-east-1 (Redwood Private / VPC). For hosted API requests that don't touch PHI, you can allow cross-region routing. We also support customer-managed KMS for Private deployments, and audit logs for every span.

[09:45] Carlos Rivera: If we pin to a Private in us-east-1, what's the failover story if that region loses power or a whole zone? We need a DR playbook that meets our RTO of 5 minutes for critical inference.
[10:08] Priya Shah: For Private deployments you can do a cold-standby in another region or an active-passive setup: replication of model artifacts and KV cache snapshots. For RTO=5m we typically recommend active-active for critical routes: run dedicated capacity in two regions with prefix-routing and health checks at the load balancer layer to failover. Active-active reduces RTO but increases cost.

[12:30] Liam O'Connor: Two technical notes: 1) KV cache consistency across regions has tradeoffs: synchronous replication kills latency and throughput, so we use eventual replication with prioritized local cache for hot prefixes, plus a consistent origin to rebuild KV when needed. 2) For throughput, quantization choices affect both memory footprint and cross-region cold-start times because quantized models reload faster.

[15:01] Maya Chen: Can you clarify KV cache rebuild times? Our peak QPS has lots of prefix locality; if failover flips traffic to new region, will we get huge latency spikes while cache rewarms?
[15:22] Priya Shah: Expect an initial spike — typical rewarm profile depends on sequence length and prefix popularity. Mitigation: 1) share a warm snapshot on failover (we push latest KV snapshot asynchronously every few minutes), 2) fast prefix caching for top N prefixes, 3) application-level retries with token-level fallback to a smaller context window. We can also provision pre-warm windows during the planned failover test.

[18:40] Carlos Rivera: About policy routing: we want split criteria — geolocation, latency SLO, remaining regional capacity, and cost. Is that all doable?
[19:02] Priya Shah: Yes. Our smart router supports compound policies: a rule tree that checks (1) request tag (PHI or non-PHI), (2) region affinity, (3) measured p95 latency to region, (4) remaining capacity percentage, then picks route. You can also set weighted traffic shifts and canary windows. Note, metrics are eventually consistent across control-plane replicas so very very tight real-time capacity decisions might lag by a few seconds.

[22:10] Anita Gupta: From security side we need audit logs for any cross-region routing decisions and SAML-based RBAC to control who can change policies. Also need proof of SOC2 controls for encryption in transit and at rest.
[22:33] Jordan Lee: We have audit trails in Redwood Console, SAML SSO and RBAC roles (admin, operator). For SOC 2, Redwood has a SOC 2 Type II report—Priya can share the compliance pack. For KMS, Private supports customer-managed keys and HSM integrations.

[25:50] Maya Chen: If we set a policy to prefer low-latency region but fall back to cheaper region when capacity is low, how do we quantify the latency vs cost tradeoff? We need a decision matrix.
[26:12] Liam O'Connor: We'll provide a cost-latency model: per-token latency distributions per region + egress pricing + dedicated overhead. Rough approach: compute expected additional tail latency when routing to alternate region vs cost delta per 1M tokens. We'll include examples for your workload (clinical summarization is latency sensitive for some routes and batch-y for others).

[29:40] Carlos Rivera: Networking: cross-region egress costs and inter-region VPC peering. If we keep PHI in-region, but use a control plane outside, are there metadata flows that could leak PII?
[30:05] Priya Shah: Control plane metadata is limited and can be configured: you can opt for private control plane in Private deployments so metadata stays in your VPC. For hosted API, we recommend filtering PII at the app-layer and using route tags to ensure PHI traffic only goes to pinned resources.

[33:55] Maya Chen: For the DR playbook, can you walk through an example sequence for a regional outage? We're looking for runbook items, who does what, and automated vs manual steps.
[34:12] Priya Shah: Sure. Example active-active playbook: (1) Automated health check triggers failover threshold when p95 degrades > X and error rate > Y. (2) Smart router reduces traffic to affected region incrementally (canary to 50% then 0%), (3) Redistribute KV read traffic to local caches while origin pulls from artifact store, (4) Ops run a verification job (synthetic requests) to validate correctness, (5) If rollout fails, rollback to previous policy and open incident. For passive-standby: (1) detection, (2) promote standby region, (3) restore KV snapshot, (4) warm prefixes, (5) update DNS / routing. We will provide a templated runbook per your SLAs.

[38:02] Anita Gupta: We also require post-incident audit with who changed policies and timestamps.

[38:12] Priya Shah: That's supported — Console logs policy changes with user and role. We can also push those logs to your SIEM via syslog or S3 export.

[41:30] Carlos Rivera: Are there known gotchas for quantized models on cold starts across regions?
[41:45] Liam O'Connor: Yes. Some quant formats reduce memory but increase CPU decode time; others are optimized for GPU kernels. Cold-start time is mostly dominated by model load and kernel init. Using smaller quantized artifacts plus preloading in standby instances reduces cold-start. Also check that both regions use compatible CUDA/cuDNN and kernel sets — mismatched driver stacks can cause performance cliffs.

[44:55] Maya Chen: We have hybrid infra: some services on-prem and some in cloud. If we use Redwood Private in our datacenter, can cross-region routing include an on-prem cluster?
[45:12] Priya Shah: Yes, Private supports on-prem nodes as a region in the router. We treat it as any region: health checks, capacity-based routing, and KV snapshots. Networking is the main challenge: ensure stable VPN/Direct Connect and consider egress/cost. Also, for on-prem you control the artifact sync cadence.

[47:30] Carlos Rivera: For testing, we want to stage a failover run. What do you need from us?
[47:42] Priya Shah: Access to staging endpoints, list of critical routes and traffic percentiles, sample synthetic workloads, and a staging account with capacity in both regions. We'll coordinate a blackout window and a rollback plan. We'll also share a checklist for pre-test validation.

[51:10] Jordan Lee: Quick note on metrics: we'll surface per-route token cost, p50/p95/p99 latencies by region, and capacity headroom. That will help you tune thresholds for policy decisions.

[53:05] Maya Chen: One operational concern: throttling behavior during failover. If we flood other regions, will we hit rate limits?
[53:18] Priya Shah: You can set soft limits and priority classes. Router will attempt to sate requests but if capacity limited, you'll see graceful degradation: queueing with timeouts, or fall through to a cheaper model variant. We can also configure circuit-breaker style policies.

[56:40] Anita Gupta: Legal/Procurement note: if we opt for multi-region Dedicated reservations, procurement will want addendum on cross-region failover SLAs.

[56:52] Jordan Lee: Noted — Jordan will work with sales to draft an addendum and provide a dedicated capacity SLA template.

[59:30] Jordan Lee: Recap and next steps: Priya to share design doc + routing policy examples; Carlos to schedule DR run; Jordan to send pricing/cost model; Redwood to provide SOC2 pack and compliance docs to Anita.

[59:58] Maya Chen: Thanks, everyone, this was helpful.

[60:05] Priya Shah: Thanks, we'll follow up with the docs today.

[60:12] Meeting end.
